The probability of detection (P) is a nonlinear function of the aircraft pose and radar position.
The radar detection model used in this work includes expressions for the probability of detection, signal-to-noise ratio, and radar cross section (RCS).
The three RCS models used in this work are constant, ellipsoid, and simple spikeball models.
The probability of detection (P) is linearized using a Taylor series expansion about a nominal operating point.
The partial derivative of P with respect to S is ∂P/∂S = √(−lnP − √(S+0.5)) / (2π(S+0.5)).
The partial derivative of S with respect to range is -c_r / (4σ_r R^5).
The partial derivative of range with respect to aircraft position is (pa - pr) / ||pa - pr||^2.
The standard deviation of the probability of detection is σ_P = √(C_P).
The lumped radar constant (c_r) used in this work is 167.4 J/m^2/°K.
The probability of false alarm (P_fa) used in this work is 1.7e-4.
The nominal range (R) used in the Monte Carlo analysis is 650 km.
The number of lobes (n) used in the simple spikeball RCS model is 4.
The amplitude of the lobes (a) used in the simple spikeball RCS model is 0.2 m^2.
The minimum RCS value (b) used in the simple spikeball RCS model is 0.15 m^2.
The aircraft pose is represented by a Gaussian distributed random variable with a mean x = (pn, Θ) and covariance C.
The radar position is assumed to be deterministic and known.
The Monte Carlo analysis consisted of 1000 runs.
